title: Multimode continuous-variable quantum key distribution with CMOS-compatible photonic-electronic integration
authors: Yiming Bian, Sarah Bastiaens, Saeed Hakimi, Huy Quang Nguyen, Aboobackkar Sidhique, Cédric Bruynsteen, Govind J. Wanjalkar, Ali Al Hadi Amhaz, Jasper Jans, Axl Bomhals, Ulrik L. Andersen, Tobias Gehring, Xin Yin, Adnan A. E. Hajomer
abstract: Multiplexing and photonic-electronic integration offer a route to scalable and high-throughput quantum key distribution (QKD) networks through parallel transmission and compact hardware suited to volume manufacturing. Realizing this route requires multichannel transmitters and receivers, and a security analysis accounting for mode coupling. Here we present a CMOS-compatible photonic-electronic multimode continuous-variable QKD architecture, using polarization multiplexing as a two-mode example. Silicon-photonic transmitter and receiver chips prepare and detect two polarization modes in parallel. The receiver is co-integrated with a dual-channel 28-nm CMOS transimpedance amplifier, providing shot-noise clearances exceeding 20 dB in both channels. Pilot-assisted unitary digital recovery removes the need for active optical polarization control, while a multimode security analysis accounts for the mode crosstalk. At 2 percent residual crosstalk, the multimode analysis extends the simulated secure distance from 39 to 84 km, near the crosstalk-free limit of 89 km. Over 10 km of deployed fibre, the mean total finite-size secret-key rate estimate is 6.69 Mbit/s, 12 percent above the single-mode analysis from the same digitally recovered data. These results establish a route to scalable multimode quantum-secured networks built on technology suited to mass production.
summary: This paper presents a CMOS-compatible, multimode architecture for continuous-variable Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) using polarization multiplexing. By developing a rigorous security analysis that accounts for mode crosstalk, the authors demonstrate a significant improvement in both secure distance and key rate compared to traditional single-mode estimates. This establishes a pathway for building scalable, mass-producible quantum-secured communication networks.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of developing scalable, high-throughput Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) networks by integrating multiple communication modes and accounting for mode coupling.
main_result: The proposed CMOS-compatible multimode architecture significantly extends the secure transmission distance (from 39 km to 84 km) and increases the key rate (by 12%) compared to single-mode analyses, proving a viable route for mass-produced quantum networks.
method: The authors combine theoretical security analysis (multimode security framework) with practical hardware implementation (CMOS-compatible silicon photonics) and digital signal processing (pilot-assisted unitary recovery).
model_or_system: The system is a dual-polarization (DP) continuous-variable QKD protocol implemented using silicon-photonic transmitters/receivers co-integrated with 28-nm CMOS transimpedance amplifiers.
key_observables: Shot-noise clearances (>20 dB), secure distance (up to 84 km), and mean total finite-size secret-key rate (6.69 Mbit/s over 10 km).
important_parameters: Residual crosstalk ($\eta_{cross} = 2\%$), modulation variances ($	ext{VMH}, 	ext{VMV}$), and the number of modes ($N$).
main_assumptions: The security analysis must consistently account for the unitary transformation applied during digital recovery, and single-mode analyses are shown to be overly conservative when mode coupling is present.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the multimode security framework, the DP CV-QKD setup, and key rate comparisons. Supporting figures detail the integrated system architecture, sideband suppression measurements, and noise spectra.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the need for scalable multimode QKD, detailing the theoretical multimode security analysis that accounts for crosstalk, presenting the integrated hardware architecture, and finally quantifying the performance gains over single-mode approaches.
why_interesting: This work directly tackles the engineering and theoretical hurdles of scaling quantum communication, providing concrete metrics and hardware blueprints for practical quantum networks, which is highly relevant to quantum information science.
